source_text: Ipsa etiam ei causa tentandi fuit Christum; quoniam more artis suae volebat capere persuadendo, cum neminem posset vitiare condendo.
pass_a_gloss: This very thing was also for him a cause of tempting Christ; because by the custom of his art he wanted to capture by persuading, since he could vitiated no one by founding.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise range; English follows the Latin without NPNF copy

pass_b_english: That was the very reason he tempted Christ: following his customary art, he wanted to capture him by persuasion, since he could corrupt no one by creating him (compare Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13) (Matthew 4:1–11) (Luke 4:1–13).

choices.english: sense taken from the locked Augustinus.it Latin
choices.why: Load-bearing wording in Julian's Latin; English follows LS/Blaise range without copying NPNF.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
